Mechanical assembly · Revision 4.3

NFC Player
Case

Putting the printed parts, the built front board and the electronics together: wood-fill sides and lid, a black front with a stainless power key, silver keys and an aluminium knob, a charcoal back, a card that leans back in a slot, and a tray in the lid for five spare cards.

200 × 128 × 59 mm printed shell. Knob, power key, screw heads, feet and cards stand proud of it; the key caps sit flush with the front.

What goes whereChangesHardwareKeys, knob and power keyAssemblyDrawings
Before you start. This guide begins with every part printed and finished. Measuring your bought parts, the fit gauge, which filament each part is printed in, slicer settings, the wood grain and staining are all in the 3D printing guide. Wiring and setting up the Pi on the bench, and building the front board, are in the electronics guide: do that first, so you know every part works before it goes in the case.

What goes where

The numbers on each picture are explained in the list under it. Hover a number or a line to pick out the other. The bought parts are simple blocks at their nominal size and position: they show where things go and which way round, not exactly what they look like.

Changes in revision 4.3

Hardware

  • M3 screws that thread straight into the print (try one in the fit gauge first, and drive by hand): four M3 × 10 for the front, four M3 × 8 for the rear, four low-profile M3 × 6 for the lid (head at most 6 mm across and 1.5 mm tall), two M3 × 6 for the card guide and two for the screen bracket, each with a washer.
  • Four M2.5 × 5 screws to hold the screen's standoffs to its bracket (check the thread of the standoffs on your screen).
  • Four M2.5 standoffs 5 mm tall, four M2.5 × 6 screws from below, and four more on top for the Pi.
  • Three M2 × 6 pan-head screws for the front board, threaded through the spacer and the key carrier and into the panel.
  • A 40-way IDC ribbon cable for the Raspberry Pi, female at both ends with both plugs on the same side of the cable (the usual kind), as short as you can find: about 10 cm. The run is about 6 cm, and a longer cable just bows upward under the lid.
  • Keys, knob and power key: four tactile switches (they go on the board), an encoder, a knob and a lit push button, all bought; the key caps are printed, all four on one key carrier. See Keys, knob and power key for exactly what to get. The front board and its parts are in the electronics guide.
  • A panel-mount USB-C socket on a short lead ending in micro-USB.
  • Four feet at least 5 mm tall. Foam pads, female-to-female jumper leads, and thin hook-up wire for the encoder and power key.

Keys, knob and power key

The keys are printed caps, all four on one printed key carrier, that press small tactile switches on the front board. The knob sits on a rotary encoder, and the power key is a panel push button with a light in it. Those are bought parts, held by the printed front panel.

What to buy

AreaChangeWhy
FrontNo brass face. The front panel is now solid, 4.2 mm thick as before, and printed in matte black PLA: its face is the finished front. The brass pocket and its rim are gone, and so is the brass template.Nothing to cut or stick by hand, and the black suits the stainless power key, the silver keys and an aluminium knob better than brass did.
Keys and knobThe key carrier is printed in silver PETG, and the knob is aluminium.To match the stainless power key.
EncoderIts pocket is unchanged, so the nut now clamps 2.3 mm of plastic where it clamped brass and plastic before.The encoder, keys, board and screen all stay exactly where they were.

PartGetMake sure
Key switches ×46 × 6 mm through-hole tactile switches, 5 mm tall with the button (often sold as "6x6x5 mm")Four legs on a 6.5 × 4.5 mm grid, and a body 3.5 mm tall. Measure one: if it is not 5 mm from its base to the top of the button, set TACT_H in case.py and rebuild, and the spacer changes to suit. Buy plenty; they come in packs.
EncoderEC11-style rotary encoder with push switch: the Pi Hut one from the electronics guide, a Bourns PEC11R or an Alps EC11An M7 threaded bushing at least 5 mm long, a 6 mm shaft that reaches at least 12 mm past the bushing, and a nut and washer (usually included). Try it in the fit gauge first.
KnobSolid aluminium knob, silver, up to 30 mm across, for a 6 mm shaftFixed with a set screw, and its bore matches your shaft's shape (D-flat or knurled).
Power key12 mm stainless panel push button, flat head, with a lit ring and power symbol (the one shown is green, 3–6 V)Momentary, not latching or self-locking. The 12.2 mm hole fits a 12 mm thread; its nut at most 16 mm across and the body at most 30 mm deep. An LED rated 3 V, or 5–6 V (those have a resistor inside: fit a wire link for R2 on the board). A 12 V or 24 V one will not light.
WireThin hook-up wire and female jumper leadsThe encoder and power key have solder tags, not connectors: solder a wire to each and finish it with a female jumper end for the board's pin headers.

How the keys feel

A short, firm press with a click after about 0.25 mm, like the buttons on hi-fi gear. The click comes from the switch: cheap packs differ, so if you want a crisper or lighter one, any 6 × 6 mm through-hole switch of the same height fits. The carrier's bridges bend as you press and add roughly 0.5 N, about a third of a typical switch's force, so the click still comes through. To make the keys lighter or firmer, change BRIDGE_T in case.py: the force goes with the cube of the thickness.

How they are held

  • Key caps: all four are one printed part, the key carrier. Its 1.2 mm frame lies on the inside of the panel, and each cap sits in its 14.4 mm square hole, face flush with the panel. Each cap hangs from two thin bridges, one above it and one below, joined to the middle of its edge by a short tab. The bridges keep it centred in its hole, so it does not rattle, and stop it falling out. A press bends them a little. The cap's back is hollow, and the switch stands inside it, 0.1 mm short of the back of the face. The switch clicks and pushes the cap back out. Two pegs on the frame sit in holes in the panel and line the carrier up. The board's screws clamp the carrier and the spacer to the panel, so take the board off to reach it.
  • Rocking: the bridges are thin enough not to dull the click, which also means they cannot stop a cap tilting if you press hard on one edge. The panel's hole still limits that, as before, to the 0.2 mm of clearance round the cap.
  • Key switches: soldered to the front of the front board, the side facing the panel. The carrier and a printed spacer between panel and board set the gap, and the board's three screws hold the lot together.
  • Encoder: held by its own nut. It goes in from behind with the threaded bushing through the 7.3 mm hole. On the front, a washer and then the nut clamp the 2.3 mm of plastic between the nut and the encoder body. The body also sits in a rectangular pocket, so it cannot turn when you twist the knob.
  • Locating lug: many encoders have a small lug beside the bushing, meant for a hole in a metal panel. The pocket already stops the encoder turning, so nip the lug off flush with side cutters, or the body will not sit flat.
  • Knob: slides onto the shaft and is held by its set screw on the shaft's flat. Leave about 1 mm between the knob and the nut so it never rubs.
  • Power key: goes in from the front through the 12.2 mm hole; its nut tightens from behind. Its body reaches past the front left corner tower, which is cut away for it between 16 and 43 mm up.
The smooth Bourns EM14 encoder mentioned in the electronics guide as a later upgrade has a different bushing and body, and needs 5 V and two resistor dividers that the board does not have. Check its drawing against the encoder hole and pocket and change ENCODER_HOLE and ENCODER_BODY in case.py, and wire it as the electronics guide describes.

Assembly

Printed part fitted in this stepPrinted parts already in placeArrow: direction of fitting

1Fit the power key, the key carrier and the encoder

Solder four wires to the power key and five to the encoder first, each ending in a female jumper end (see What plugs in where in the electronics guide). It is easier before they are in the panel. Then:

  1. Push the power key in from the front and tighten its nut from behind, with its tags pointing down or sideways.
  2. Lay the panel face down. Lay the key carrier on it, caps down, so each cap drops into its hole and the two pegs into their holes. The frame then lies flat on the panel. From the front, left to right, the keys read previous, play/pause, next, back. Press each cap from the front: it should move in a little and spring back, without catching on the sides of its hole.
  3. Nip off the encoder's locating lug if it has one. From behind, put the bushing through its hole so the body drops into the rectangular pocket.
  4. On the front: washer, then nut. Tighten the nut firmly with a spanner, holding the body square in its pocket.
  5. Slide the knob on, leaving about 1 mm clear of the nut, and tighten its set screw onto the flat of the shaft.

2Fit the spacer and the front board

  1. Build the board first: see Front board for the case in the electronics guide.
  2. Press the ribbon's plug onto the board's box header now, red stripe at the triangle. It is hard to reach once the board is on.
  3. With the panel still face down and the carrier in place, lay the spacer on the carrier, its screw holes over the carrier's.
  4. Lay the board on the spacer, switches down towards the caps (see the close-up of one key).
  5. Fit its three M2 × 6 screws, snug only: they thread into the spacer and the panel.
  6. Turn it over and press each key: it should click, and spring back flush. A key that is already pressed in or rattles means a switch of a different height; see TACT_H under Measure first.

3Fit the front panel and the screen

  1. Screw the front panel to the chassis with four M3 × 10 screws. The power key's body passes the front left corner tower through its notch.
  2. Leave the four brass standoffs on the screen board. Screw the board to the bracket from behind with four M2.5 screws through the standoffs, glass facing away from the bracket and the socket on its open side. Leave them a little loose.
  3. Stand the bracket behind the window, socket on the right by the knob, and put its two M3 × 6 screws and washers through the base's slots into the floor bosses, loosely.
  4. Push the bracket forward until the glass touches the panel, then tighten its two floor screws.
  5. Look through the window and slide the screen sideways in its slots until the lit area is centred, then tighten its four screws.
  6. Push the lead's plug into the socket from the right, then bend the wires back towards the rear, clear of the encoder. A foam pad between the bracket and the lid stops it rattling.

4Mount the Pi and the DAC

  1. Screw four standoffs up through the two floor slots and leave them loose.
  2. Screw the Pi onto them, header at the front. Plug the DAC straight onto the Pi, checking pin 1. The pins of its header stand up through it, ready for the ribbon.
  3. Slide the stack back until the DAC's rear edge is {n(c.DAC_GAP)} mm from the rear panel's place (hold the panel on to check the sockets line up with its holes), then tighten the standoffs from below.

5Fit the card guide and the NFC reader

  1. Screw the guide to the two floor bosses with M3 × 6 screws. The slot leans back toward the top.
  2. Set the reader's switches for SPI. Slide it down into the middle pair of grooves in the two posts, antenna side toward the card and header at the top. That holds it 20 mm behind the card, where it reads best; this reader misses cards held right against it.
  3. Try a card. If reads are unreliable, move the reader to the front or rear grooves (16 or 24 mm). The lid stops it lifting out, so no tie or glue is needed.

6Wire it

  1. Run the ribbon straight back from the board and bend it down onto the pins on top of the DAC, red stripe on pin 1. It needs no twist and no fold. The DAC has no notch, so check first: pin 1 is the corner pin with a square pad on the Pi, at the right-hand end seen from the front of the case. With the Pi running it reads 3.3 V, and its neighbour across the header (pin 2) reads 5 V.
  2. Plug the leads into the board's headers as What plugs in where in the electronics guide says: screen to LCD, reader to NFC, knob to ENC, power key to PWR.
  3. Keep the ribbon and leads out from under the card tray, which comes down to 52 mm over the left two thirds of the case, and clear of the card slot. Leave enough slack that the front panel can come off with everything attached.
  4. Before closing up, run the checks in the electronics guide: every key, the knob, the power key and its light, the screen and a card.

7Fit the rear panel

  1. Mount the USB-C socket in the rear panel and plug its lead into the Pi port marked USB (not PWR IN).
  2. Screw the rear panel on with four M3 × 8 screws.
  3. Check that an RCA plug and a headphone plug both seat fully through their holes.

8Close up

  1. Before closing for good, test card reading with the front fitted and five cards in the tray.
  2. Lower the lid between the panels and fit its four low-profile screws, by hand.
  3. Stick the feet on, clear of the floor slots and the vents.
